# The Operations Loop

The system must be able to coordinate its own work. This means a closed loop:

**Planning** → **Dispatch** → **Execution** → **Tracking** → **Review** → **Feedback/Adjustment** → Planning again.

Each stage is a full capability, not a feature. Each stage's output is the next stage's input. The loop applies at every scale — a single session, a week, a quarter, a generation. The work type classification (process/procedure/derivation/inquiry — and possibly others not yet identified) governs what kind of work each stage handles, and the settlement path (work becoming more determined over time) applies to the loop itself.

Without this loop, the system cannot:
- Answer "what should I work on today?"
- Tell you whether plans are on track
- Learn from what went well or badly
- Coordinate work across sessions, people, or time horizons
- Do any of the things the endeavor requires at enterprise/government grade

This is not project management software bolted on. This is the endeavor's circulatory system — the way work flows through the organization. Every other capability (ERP, research publication, healthcare, physical infrastructure) depends on this loop functioning, because every capability requires coordinated work to build and operate.

## What exists now

Partial implementations of some stages:
- **Planning:** compute-plan-status.js, task files with dependencies and work types, plan/project/objective hierarchy. No scheduling, no time, no capacity.
- **Dispatch:** agent definitions, /dispatch and /orchestrate commands. No work-type routing, no assignment tracking, no authority enforcement.
- **Execution:** hooks monitoring tool use, session infrastructure. No execution state machine, no artifact tracking, no WIP limits.
- **Tracking:** status fields on tasks, compute-plan-status rollup. No metrics, no history, no audit trail.
- **Review:** code-review command, observer agent, evaluate-session hook. No retrospectives, no plan-vs-actual, no approval gates.
- **Feedback:** instinct/skill/hook maturation pipeline, memory system, /learn command. No feedback-to-plan pipeline, no experiment framework.

## What's missing from the vocabulary

The library's work domain has ~20 clean, usable terms and ~15 more with extractable concepts buried in math formalization. But roughly 35-40 concepts needed for the full loop have no term at all — schedule, milestone, deadline, assignment, queue, execution state, artifact, status, progress, metric, review, cadence, and many others.

The four work types (process/procedure/derivation/inquiry) may not be exhaustive. Research may surface additional types or a different classification altogether.

## Scale

This is the largest single piece of work in the system. Estimated 75-150 tasks across 6+ plans, with research phases that are genuine inquiry (we don't know what we need until we study the literature) and build phases that are procedure (known goal, implementation requires judgment). The research must come first — terms must be grounded in real disciplines before infrastructure is built on them.
"}

# Work Operations: The Six-Stage Loop

This project builds the system's ability to coordinate work as one integrated system.

## Why this is one project, not six

Planning without tracking is guessing. Tracking without execution data is fiction. Review without plan-vs-actual comparison is venting. Feedback without plan adjustment is journaling. The six stages share a data model — work units flow through all of them. Building them separately produces six disconnected tools. Building them together produces a circulatory system.

The connective tissue is:
- **Work units** are both the output of Execution and the input to Tracking
- **Plans** are both the output of Planning/Feedback and the input to Dispatch
- **Status** is both the output of Tracking and the input to Review
- **Adjustments** are both the output of Feedback and the input to Planning
- **Events** (state transitions, completions, failures, approvals) are the data that flows between all stages

## Plan structure

### 1. ops-research-foundations
Research across all declared required stages in parallel. Read the real literature on scheduling, dispatch/delegation, execution monitoring, metrics, retrospectives, continuous improvement. Produce survey texts grounded in real sources. This is genuine inquiry — we don't know what terms we need until we study what practitioners and researchers have learned.

### 2. ops-vocabulary
Define the terms the loop needs, grounded in the research. This includes terms we know we need (schedule, milestone, assignment, execution state, metric, review, cadence, etc.) and terms the research surfaces that we haven't anticipated. Also: evaluate whether the four work types are exhaustive or need expansion.

### 3-8. Stage-specific plans (one per stage)
Each stage gets its own plan covering: frontmatter schema for that stage's records, tools/commands for that stage, hooks for enforcement, integration points with adjacent stages. Each depends on the vocabulary being defined first.

### 9. ops-integration
The cross-cutting plan: the event model, the state machine, the flow concept, the multi-scale operation (how the same loop works for a session and for a generation). This runs alongside the stage plans, not after them — integration is designed continuously, not bolted on at the end.

## What this subsumes

The existing planning-infrastructure plan should be absorbed into ops-planning-stage once the research foundations are complete. Much of its content is valid but needs to be part of the larger structure rather than standing alone.

Tasks from agentic-orchestration that touch the operations loop (operationalize-work-vocabulary, work-hierarchy-enforcement, parameterizable-record-commands, frontmatter-consequence-hook) should be coordinated with this project's plans.

## Research-first

Every stage starts with research. The terms come from the research. The schemas come from the terms. The tools come from the schemas. This ordering is not optional — building tools on undefined vocabulary is how you get slop.

# Multi-Scale Operations

The loop must work at:
- **Session scale** — what am I doing right now, what's blocked, what did I just finish
- **Daily scale** — what's planned for today, standup
- **Weekly scale** — what happened this week, what's next week, weekly review
- **Monthly scale** — progress against objectives, monthly retro
- **Quarterly scale** — project-level review, objective adjustment
- **Annual scale** — goal-level review, direction setting
- **Generational scale** — seven-generations thinking, long-horizon planning

These are not seven different systems. They're the same loop operating at different cadences, with information rolling up and down. A session's completed tasks roll up into a week's progress. A quarter's review rolls down into next quarter's plan. The generational horizon constrains what the quarterly plans can aim for.

This requires research we haven't done — particularly the seven-generations thinking from Haudenosaunee governance, which is a fundamentally different approach to temporal planning than anything in Western project management literature.

All eight research tasks can run in parallel. Each produces a survey text in the library. Each must read real sources — academic papers, practitioner literature, standards documents, indigenous governance traditions — not summarize Wikipedia or regurgitate productivity blogs.

- GTD: Allen (2001/2015) — the five stages, weekly review, next actions, contexts

- Bratman (*Intention, Plans, and Practical Reason* 1987) — already in plan.md but needs deeper engagement

# Foundational Ontology: Enrich Core Terms and Fill Gaps

## The problem

The foundational terms at `library/terms/` are what everything else builds on. Thing, object, quality, state, act, vessel, container — these are the primitives that the work domain, the operations loop, the app specs, and eventually the whole relational computer depend on.

14 of 23 terms are solid. 9 are one-sentence stubs. And several critical terms don't exist at all.

The thin stubs include the most load-bearing concepts:
- **act** (1 line: "a manifestation of a thing's energy resulting in change") — every operation, every task execution, every state transition IS an act
- **quality** (1 line: "any component of a thing which can be observed or measured") — every frontmatter field IS a quality of a thing
- **state** (1 line: "the composite of all conditions defining a thing at a moment") — every task status, every execution state IS a state
- **condition** (1 line) — every precondition, completion condition, guard in a procedure IS a condition

You can't build a rigorous operations loop on one-sentence definitions of its primitives.

## Missing terms

These concepts are referenced by existing terms but have no definition:
- **relation** — connections between things. Defined in math (binary-relation.md) but not at the foundational level. Every dependency, every assignment, every membership IS a relation.
- **event** — an act that happened at a specific time. Every status change, every completion, every failure IS an event. The operations loop runs on events.
- **change** — referenced by act.md ("resulting in change") but undefined. The fundamental thing that acts produce.
- **time** / **moment** — referenced by state.md ("at a given moment in time") but undefined. The dimension that makes state meaningful and events possible.
- **property** — related to quality but distinct. A quality you can observe; a property a thing has whether or not you observe it. Frontmatter fields are properties.
- **identity** — what makes a thing THIS thing and not another. Referenced implicitly everywhere (a task's id, a file's path, a person's name). The foundational concept behind `id:` in frontmatter.

The research task may surface others.

## The critical path

```
research-foundational-ontology (inquiry)
  ↓ unblocks all enrichment/addition tasks (derivation — follow writing-terms, meaning from research)
    ↓ unblocks research-ops-ontology-mapping (how the ontology applies to work)
      ↓ unblocks all other operations loop research
        ↓ unblocks ops-vocabulary
          ↓ unblocks all stage-specific plans
```

The research task is the single point of entry. Everything else fans out from it.

## What "solid" means

Each enriched/new term should match the quality of thing.md, object.md, vessel.md, container.md:
- Multiple paragraphs explaining what the concept IS
- Grounded in at least one external source (Aristotle, philosophy of action, temporal logic, etc.)
- Distinguished from adjacent concepts
- Connected to other foundational terms via links and frontmatter
- Written for a smart reader with no background
- Useful as a foundation that domain-specific terms can build on

**Action:** Research the foundational concepts that everything in the repo builds on. Read the real sources on ontological primitives — what are things, qualities, states, acts, relations, events, change, time, identity?

**Why:** The foundational terms are load-bearing. Act, quality, state, condition are one-sentence stubs. Relation, event, change, time don't exist. Every domain-specific term (task, plan, milestone, assignment) is a specialization of these primitives. If the primitives are thin, everything built on them is ungrounded.

**Key sources:**
- Aristotle, *Categories* — substance, quality, quantity, relation, place, time, position, state, action, passion. The original ten categories. Our "thing" maps to substance, our "quality" maps to quality, our "act" maps to action/passion, our "state" maps to state/condition.
- Aristotle, *Metaphysics* — potentiality and actuality (δύναμις and ἐνέργεια). An act is the realization of a potentiality. A state is an actuality. Change is the transition from potentiality to actuality.
- Aristotle, *Physics* IV — time, place, void. Time as "the number of motion with respect to before and after." State requires a moment; event requires a temporal interval.
- Locke, *Essay Concerning Human Understanding* II — primary vs. secondary qualities. Properties a thing has vs. qualities an observer perceives.
- Whitehead, *Process and Reality* (1929) — actual occasions, process ontology. Events as primary, objects as derived. The repo already has a process philosophy text.
- Kim, *Supervenience and Mind* (1993) — events as property exemplifications at times. The standard analytic philosophy account of events.
- Davidson, *Essays on Actions and Events* (1980) — what individuates events? When are two descriptions descriptions of the same event?
- Galton & Mizoguchi (2009) "The water falls but the waterfall does not fall" — the ontology of events, processes, and states in applied ontology
- DOLCE (Descriptive Ontology for Linguistic and Cognitive Engineering) — a formal foundational ontology used in knowledge engineering
- BFO (Basic Formal Ontology) — the ontology used in biomedical informatics; distinguishes continuants (things that persist) from occurrents (things that happen)
- The existing `library/terms/` — what do the solid terms (thing, object, vessel, container) already assume about these primitives?
- TAB (Things with Attributes and Behaviors) — the MUD ontology already referenced in thing.md. What does it assume?

**Key questions:**
- Is our thing/object/quality/state/act decomposition the right one, or does it need revision?
- What's the relationship between quality and property? Between state and condition?
- What IS an event, and how does it differ from an act? (An event is an act located in time?)
- What IS change, and how does it relate to state? (Change is a transition between states?)
- What IS time in a flatfile system where everything is versioned by git commits?
- What IS identity for an entity that's a markdown file? (The file path? The id field? Something else?)
- How do formal ontologies (DOLCE, BFO) handle the thing/event distinction? Can we learn from them without importing their full complexity?
"}

**Action:** Research the repo's own foundational ontology — emsenn's relational, processual philosophy as expressed in the predication paper, the relationality spec, and the existing `library/terms/`. Read these FIRST. Then read Western ontology (Aristotle, Whitehead, etc.) as contrast and lineage — to clarify where the relational framework agrees, disagrees, and goes further.

**Why:** The foundational terms are load-bearing. Act, quality, state, condition are one-sentence stubs. Relation, event, change, time don't exist. Every domain-specific term (task, plan, milestone, assignment) is a specialization of these primitives. The primitives must be grounded in the repo's own philosophy — which is relational and processual, not substance-based.

**Primary sources (the repo's own theory):**
- The predication paper: `library/domains/science/domains/information/texts/the-adjoint-structure-of-predication-on-bilattice-valued-fibers.md` — the mathematical foundation. Predication as adjunction. Extending and restricting as residuals.
- The relationality spec: `library/domains/science/domains/relationality/relationality.md` — acts as reflexive witnessing, the trace calculus, closure-flow-shuffle
- The existing `library/terms/` — thing, object, quality, state, act, vessel, container. What do these already assume? Where are they relational vs. accidentally Aristotelian?
- Process philosophy text: `library/domains/humanities/domains/philosophy/domains/western/domains/metaphysics/domains/process-philosophy/texts/process-and-relational-ontology.md`
- TAB (Things with Attributes and Behaviors) — referenced in thing.md. The MUD ontology.
- emsenn's babbles — for the philosophical intuitions behind the formal work

**Contrast sources (Western ontology as lineage, not authority):**
- Aristotle, *Categories* — the ten categories as the classical starting point. Where the relational framework departs: thing is not substance (it's anything distinguishable), act is not energeia (it's reflexive witnessing), quality is not an accident of substance (it's an observable component of a relational entity)
- Whitehead, *Process and Reality* (1929) — process philosophy, actual occasions. Closer to the relational framework than Aristotle. Where it aligns and where it differs.
- Peirce — semiotics, thirdness, relational logic. Already part of the repo's lineage (inquiry.md cites Peirce)
- Locke — primary/secondary qualities. Useful contrast for the quality/property distinction.
- DOLCE, BFO — formal foundational ontologies from knowledge engineering. How they solve the same problems. What we can learn from their distinctions (continuant/occurrent, endurant/perdurant) without importing their substance-based assumptions.

**Practical sources (how MUDs and game engines model this):**
- LPC, MOO, Evennia — MUD object models. How text worlds solve entity/property/state/action modeling.
- Entity-Component-System (ECS) — game dev pattern. Entities as IDs, components as data, systems as behavior.
- Evans, *Domain-Driven Design* (2003) — entities, value objects, aggregates.

**Key questions:**
- What does the relational framework say about what a thing IS? (Not substance — what then?)
- What does reflexive witnessing mean for acts? How does this differ from Aristotle's action/passion?
- Is the thing/quality/state/act decomposition adequate FOR the relational framework, or does it smuggle in Aristotelian assumptions?
- What does time mean in a relational/processual ontology? (Not "the number of motion" — what?)
- What does identity mean when things are constituted by relations, not by substance?
- What does change mean when process is primary and objects are derivative?
- How does the predication adjunction (extending/restricting) relate to the foundational terms?
- Where do the MUD/game-engine models align with the relational framework? Where do they assume substance ontology that we shouldn't?

# The Relational MUD

The interface to the system is a MUD. You log in, you walk around, you look at things, you tell your party (agents) what to do. The library IS the world — domains are rooms, terms are objects, texts are documents you can read. The operations loop entities (tasks, plans, projects) live in the same world as the knowledge entities. Looking at a task in the MUD isn't reading a file — it's encountering an entity.

This is not a toy or a skin over file operations. The MUD IS the relational computer's interaction paradigm:
- The library's domain hierarchy IS the room graph
- Frontmatter fields ARE attributes on things
- Skills ARE behaviors (TAB's behavior files map to skills)
- Commands ARE commands (TAB's command files map to slash commands)
- The agent IS an NPC in your party who can act on your behalf
- System relationships (TAB's role system) map to office/delegation
- The dimension IS the running system

The TAB architecture (Things with Attributes and Behaviors) already exists — emsenn wrote it across multiple MUD engines (qtMUD, Racket-MUD, Fennel/TAB). The 10 persistent patterns across a decade of rewrites are the skeleton. The triage documents above contain detailed architecture notes.

## How this connects

- **Foundational ontology**: thing/object/quality/state/act/vessel/container ARE the MUD entity hierarchy
- **Operations loop**: the MUD is the interface to plan/dispatch/execute/track/review/adjust
- **Work operations**: walking into a project room and saying "what's ready?" IS compute-plan-status
- **Agential realism (Barad)**: observation and phenomenon aren't separate — looking at a task IS an intra-action with it
- **FARS**: the on-disk world. TAB is in-memory; FARS is on-disk. Same architecture, different persistence.
- **Kind system**: TAB models (thing → object → mobile → person) map to FARS kinds with SHACL validation

## What exists

- TAB engine code in triage (Fennel, Python, Racket versions)
- Detailed architecture research (tab-mud-research.md)
- Kind/engine design doc (thing-kind-and-engine-as-tab.md)
- MUD heritage analysis (mud-heritage-as-practice-derivation.md)
- The foundational terms (thing.md, object.md, vessel.md, container.md) are already written in MUD style
- Claude Code agents already function as party NPCs — you tell them what to do

## What this project needs to figure out

- What's the actual runtime? Fennel/Lua? Node.js? Something else?
- How does the MUD connect to the flatfile substrate? (TAB is in-memory, FARS is on-disk — the bridge is the key problem)
- How does the kind system work? (thing-kind-and-engine-as-tab.md sketches SHACL shapes)
- What's the minimum viable MUD that's useful? (Log in, walk around library, look at things, talk to agent)
